Senses.Explanation: The graph names a buddha and, with the article, the Buddha. It occurs 116,053 times in 459 allowlisted texts, but the Chan record gives this extremely broad title a sharply observable deployment of its own. The Buddha in the lineage-opening scenes is a participant in public actions: the World-Honored One mounts the seat, Kashyapa announces that the Buddha has finished speaking, and the Buddha leaves the seat; at Vulture Peak he holds up a flower before the silent assembly and Kashyapa smiles. The same bare word is made the object of the stock public question "What is Buddha?" (如何是佛), to which the records preserve mutually different answers rather than a common descriptive biography: Yunmen says "a dry shit-stick" (乾屎橛), Dongshan says "three catties of hemp" (麻三斤), and Huangbo says "this very mind is buddha; no-mind is the Way" (即心是佛，無心是道). Linji supplies an explicit formula in answer to "What are the true buddha, true teaching, and true Way?": "buddha is the mind's purity; the teaching is the mind's brightness; the Way is unobstructed pure light everywhere" (佛者，心清淨是；法者，心光明是；道者，處處無礙淨光是), then calls all three empty names without real existence (三即一，皆是空名，而無寔有). The corpus also turns against the title itself. Zhaozhou's recorded saying is "the one word 'buddha'—I do not like to hear it" (佛之一字，吾不喜聞). A lamp record attributes to Deshan a longer roster beginning "here there is no buddha and no patriarch" (這裏佛也無，祖也無) and ending "buddha is an old barbarian's shit-stick" (佛是老胡屎橛). Linji places buddha first in a five-part roster of whatever one meets inside or outside: "meet a buddha, kill the buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" (逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷). Later comments keep the lineage-opening scene open to appraisal: Dongshan Shouchu says people know only the flower and smile but do not know the World-Honored One, while Yulin calls the flower and smile the single transmission of the treasury of the true teaching eye and says it has made clear-eyed people laugh ever since. This is where Chan bends the word: its Buddha is recorded through the flower and teaching-seat actions, answers and self-formulas in public exchanges, refusal and abuse of the title, later appraisal of the lineage-opening scene, and the title's place in a killing roster—not through an outside religious life story.
Senses.Note: This sense covers the figure/title and the word as deployed in Chan, not the physical image separated below. Longer compounds keep their own articles and should not be silently substituted for it: 'buddha-nature' (佛性); the question 'What is Buddha?' (如何是佛); 'this very mind is buddha' (即心是佛); 'meet a buddha, kill the buddha' (逢佛殺佛); and 'denounce buddhas and revile patriarchs' (呵佛罵祖). The graph 'buddha' (佛) in 'the Buddha's teaching' (佛法) is also a compound constituent and does not by itself justify leaving the entire compound untranslated. The curated evidence spans an early lamp compilation, Linji's own record, and Huangbo's record; later compilations and commentaries repeatedly preserve and comment on the same scenes and formulas.

Senses.Explanation: The same bare graph can name a physical buddha image rather than a person or title. The Record of the Chan Gate's Forged Reflections lists the twenty-fifth case as “Danxia burns a buddha” (丹霞燒佛). An independent allowlisted record names the same Danxia burning case with the material object explicit: “Danxia burns a wooden buddha” (丹霞燒木佛). The shortened and expanded case names therefore identify the burned buddha as a wooden image. This is a different object from the buddha addressed, questioned, rejected, or invoked in the primary sense, so the image receives its own sense rather than being folded into a reading of the title.
Senses.Note: The exact shortened form is anchored beside an independent expanded case name that makes the wooden-image referent explicit. Cross-checking the wooden-buddha family confirms the material referent: records say Danxia burned a wooden buddha for warmth, ask how a wooden buddha could contain relics, and contrast gold, wood, clay, and the 'true buddha.' The longer compound 'wooden buddha' (木佛) remains a related entry rather than replacing this bare-word sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二十五、丹霞燒佛

Occurrences.Kwic: 丹霞燒木佛

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “buddha” (佛), and the second means “nature” (性): 'buddha-nature.' The term reaches the Chan record as a sutra line the masters quote and put in play — (一切眾生皆有佛性) ('all sentient beings have buddha-nature'): Yanguan Qi'an preaches the line straight to his assembly, and it stands inside the stock phrase (見性成佛) ('see the nature, become buddha'). The corpus also records the term against social rank: told a 'Lingnan barbarian has no Buddha-nature,' Huineng answers (人則有南北)，(佛性無南北) ('people may be north or south, but Buddha-nature is neither north nor south'). The record's most-repeated instruction bearing the term is given as a scripture quotation in Baizhang's mouth at Guishan's awakening over the stirred ember (五燈會元, 溈山靈祐 chapter): (經云)。(欲識佛性義)。(當觀時節因緣)。(時節既至)。(如迷忽悟) ('the sutra says: if you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, observe times and conditions; when the time arrives, it is like waking suddenly from delusion') — the clause (欲識佛性義) recurs 178x in 103 allowlist texts. The word is also put as a test-question, (如何是佛性) ('what is buddha-nature?', 43x/32): (普明大師) (Great Master Puming) answers a monk (汝無佛性) ('you have no buddha-nature') and, pressed with (蠢動含靈皆有佛性學人為何却無) ('wriggling and sentient creatures all have buddha-nature — why do I alone lack it?'), grounds it (為汝向外求) ('because you seek outward', 傳燈玉英集); one master answers (誰無)？ ('who lacks it?') where another answers (誰有)？ ('who has it?', 象田即念禪師語錄); an emperor's asking is answered (不離陛下所問) ('not apart from what Your Majesty is asking') — (帝乃問如何是佛性師曰不離陛下所問帝默契) ('the emperor asked: what is buddha-nature? the master said: not apart from what Your Majesty is asking; the emperor silently accorded', 禪宗頌古聯珠通集). A recurring test poses the earthworm cut in two — (蚯蚓斬為兩段)，(兩頭俱動)，(未審佛性在阿那頭) ('an earthworm is cut in two and both ends move: in which end is the buddha-nature?'): (延慶法端) (Yanqing Faduan) spreads both hands (師展兩手, 景德傳燈錄), while (長沙景岑) (Changsha Jingcen) answers (莫妄想) ('no fantasizing') and, pressed (爭柰動何) ('but what about the moving?'), says (會即風火未散) ('understand: the wind and fire have not yet dispersed', 聯燈會要). (仰山問中邑)：「(如何是佛性義)？」 ('Yangshan asked Zhongyi: what is the meaning of buddha-nature?') draws the simile (如室有六窗)，(中安一獼猴) ('like a room with six windows and a monkey placed inside'; raised in 宏智覺禪師語錄 and repeatedly after). The question frame (還有佛性也無) ('does it have buddha-nature or not?') recurs 334x/123 (counting 有佛性也無). The same corpus-wide headword is also deployed in Zhaozhou's dog case. A monk quotes the statement 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature' (一切眾生皆有佛性) and asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature. Zhaozhou answers, 'no' (無). Pressed—'from the buddhas down to ants everything has it; why not a dog?'—he says, 'because it has action-consciousness nature' (為伊有業識性在). Elsewhere he answers 'yes' (有) for a cypress tree, and once answers, 'every gate opens onto the road to Chang'an' (家家門前通長安). Zhaozhou also groups buddha-nature, awakening, extinction, and true thusness (佛性、菩提、涅槃、真如) as 'clothes worn against the skin—also called vexations' (貼體衣服，亦名煩惱). Guishan makes a related inversion for a whole assembly: 'no sentient being has buddha-nature' (一切眾生皆無佛性). The word 'no' is what a later record tells its addressee to look at: Dahui says to look at the saying (看箇話頭)—a monk asked Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature, and Zhaozhou said no—and to keep raising it at all times (時時提掇). The case is case 1 of the Wumenguan. It circulates as 'the dog's buddha-nature' (狗子佛性, 217 hits in 77 allowlisted texts) and 'the dog has no buddha-nature' (狗子無佛性, 427 in 119); 'does a dog have buddha-nature?' (狗子還有佛性) recurs 277 times in 110 texts. The bare answer is called 'the word no' (無字, 801 raw string matches across 173 texts) and 'Zhaozhou's word no' (趙州無字, 77 in 35).
Senses.Note: This sense records the sutra line as the record quotes and deploys it — reported as the texts' quotation, not as this entry's claim about what beings have. Zhaozhou's dog-case deployment belongs to this same corpus-wide sense. Zen-scoped counts: (佛性) 4,137x in 363 allowlist texts; (一切眾生皆有佛性) 64x/46; (欲識佛性義) 178x/103 (its continuation 當觀時節因緣 'observe times and conditions' 229x/124); (如何是佛性) ('what is buddha-nature?') 43x/32; the earthworm test (蚯蚓斬)… 16x/13 (佛性在阿那頭 'in which end is the buddha-nature' 18x/9). Anchors for quotes in the Explanation: Baizhang/Guishan X80n1565 ed="X" lb 0185a22; (普明大師) B14n0082 (傳燈玉英集) lb 0254b12; (法端) T51n2076 lb 0284c06; emperor exchange C078n1720 lb 0684a22; (仰山)/(中邑) J32nB272 lb 0195b07. He answers (有) ('yes') for a cypress and lumps (佛性) with (菩提)、(涅槃)、(真如) (awakening, nirvana, true thusness) as (貼體衣服)，(亦名煩惱) ('clothing worn against the skin — also called vexations'). The assembly-wide inversion (一切眾生皆無佛性) ('no sentient being has buddha-nature') recurs 13x in 6 allowlist texts.

AlternateTargets: how is my hand like the Buddha's hand?
Senses.Explanation: The stock 'Buddha-hand' term names one of Huanglong Huinan's three public-interview barriers. Huanglong asks where the monk's native connection is, stretches out his hand and asks, 'how is my hand like the Buddha's hand?', then lowers his foot and asks how it resembles a donkey's foot. Records say he posed the three for over thirty years and that communities called them Huanglong's Three Barriers. Later masters answer, verse, criticize, and re-ask the Buddha-hand question. Zen thus bends an ordinary possessive phrase into a short case-name for a recurring public-interview checkpoint.
Senses.Note: The question, Buddha-hand/donkey-foot/native-connection set, and Huanglong's Three Barriers converge on this named lexical object. Fingered citron and Buddha-hand Rock are separate compounds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師室中常問僧曰：人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處？正當問答交鋒，却復伸手曰：我手何似佛手？又問諸方參請宗師所得，却復垂脚曰：我脚何似驢脚？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing account places the Buddha-hand question in a chamber interview.

Senses.Explanation: Literally kudzu-and-wisteria creepers — vines that twist, cling and choke. In Chan it is the standing metaphor for WORDS that entangle: talk, verbiage, verbal complication, the case (公案) as a thicket of language. Yuanwu equates it outright with speech — (那裏如此葛藤)。(須是斬斷語言) 'why all this vine-tangle here? one must cut off words.' A teacher who explains too much is (打葛藤) 'spinning out vines'; the cases themselves are (葛藤公案) 'vine-tangle cases'; merely wordy Chan is disparaged as (葛藤禪) 'vine-Chan' (one pejorative label in a whole doxographic list of bad 'Chans'). The word carries a negative, self-deprecating cast — even a master opening a talk calls it (與諸人葛藤) 'getting tangled up in vines with you all.' It names the tangle of language, which the texts speak of cutting through (截斷／斬斷葛藤). The deployment range is wide: (截斷葛藤) ('cut off the vines') is spoken as a standalone dismissal in live exchanges — (師以拄杖畫一畫云)。(截斷葛藤) ('the master drew one stroke with his staff and said: cut off the vines'), (喝一喝)。(截斷葛藤) ('gave a shout: cut off the vines'); the tangle is a nest one sits or crashes into, (葛藤窠) — (坐在葛藤窠裡) ('sitting in the vine-nest'), (商量也依前撞入葛藤窠) ('discuss it and you crash into the vine-nest as before'); and the label reaches all the way up to the canon itself — (一大藏教閑葛藤)。(千七百則絆殺人) ('the whole great treasury of the teachings: idle vine-tangle; the seventeen hundred cases trip men to death'), and independently (一大藏教閑葛藤)。(盡大地人跳不出) ('idle vine-tangle the whole earth's people cannot jump clear of').
Senses.Note: Single corpus-wide metaphorical sense. The literal botanical 'kudzu vine' underlies it but in the Zen records the term is almost always the figurative 'verbal entanglement.' Counts (462-text allowlist grep): (葛藤) 2530 hits in 334 of the 462 texts; (打葛藤) 188 in 98; (葛藤窠) 144 in 81 (坐在葛藤窠裡 J10nA158 0004b05; 撞入葛藤窠 C078n1720 0669b19); (截斷葛藤) 80 in 60 (staff-stroke dismissals J25nB171 0519a07, 0535c08; 喝一喝 J26nB177 0038c28); (葛藤露布) 33 in 27; (葛藤禪) 21 in 18; (閑葛藤) 5 in 5 (一大藏教閑葛藤 J34nB299 0126a19 and X71n1420 0640a07).

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。事不獲已。與諸人葛藤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), head (杭州慶善院普能禪師): 'Taking the hall — unavoidably, I'll spin out vines with you all.' A master's self-deprecating opening; (與諸人葛藤) = deal you some verbiage.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "empty" or "vacant" (虛) "space" (空): "empty space," also the open sky, attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it as a location, comparison, and grammatical object. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 90 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.
Senses.Note: The headword spans ordinary spatial reference, comparisons, verse imagery, questions, and compounds. The curated witnesses foreground recurrent Chan deployment rather than the hundreds of scholastic similes in one prolific compilation. The exact graph pair remains "empty space" even where English idiom favors "sky."

Occurrences.Kwic: 此一瓣香虛空包不住。大地載不起。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's incense statement: "this one petal of incense cannot be contained by empty space or supported by the great earth."

Occurrences.Kwic: 者裏明得，虛空可量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an Fan's formal address: "if understood here, empty space can be measured." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉頭頓忘迷悟如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Memorial narrative: "raising his head, he suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, lucid like empty space and impossible to approach or lodge in." Historical narration remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「待虛空粉碎來向汝道。」云：「粉碎後如何？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In public exchange, the master postpones his answer until empty space shatters, and the monk asks what follows the shattering.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。一棒打破虛空。進云。過在什麼處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master answers a request for the upward road with one blow that breaks empty space; the questioner immediately asks where the fault lies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 虛空無內外，心法亦如是。若了虛空故，是達真如理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmitted verse predicates that empty space has neither inside nor outside and uses it as the stated comparison for mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫向虛空裏釘橛有一屠兒身上常出乳香舍利
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A comment warns against driving a stake into empty space before introducing the butcher account.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你若揀辨，大似虛空中畫疆界；你若不揀辨，又是漆桶裏坐墨煤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address compares discriminating there to drawing territorial boundaries in empty space, then gives the contrary warning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾請偈，師不荅。將二鼓，復索筆書曰：一燈在望，更無言說。大地平沉，虛空迸裂。書畢，泊然而寂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At the assembly's request, a dying master writes a final verse in which the great earth sinks flat and empty space bursts apart, then dies peacefully.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：達磨正宗，衲僧巴鼻。充塞虛空，無處回避。堪笑迷流，白日青天開却眼，只管瞌睡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address says that Bodhidharma's true lineage, the Chan monk's defining feature, fills empty space and leaves nowhere to evade it.
